text:
Verses 26-36

(7:26) O Children of Adam! We have certainly sent down to you garments to cover your shameful parts, and adornments. Yet the

garment of Godwariness—that is better. That is [one] of Allah’s signs, so that they may take admonition.

(7:27) O Children of Adam! Do not let Satan tempt you, like he expelled your parents from paradise, stripping them of their garments to expose to them their shameful parts. Indeed he sees you—he and his hosts—whence you do not see them. We have indeed made the devils guardians of those who have no faith.

(7:28) When they commit an indecency, they say, “We found our fathers practicing it, and Allah has enjoined it upon us.” Say, “Indeed Allah does not enjoin indecencies. Do you attribute to Allah what you do not know?”

(7:29) Say, “My Lord has enjoined justice,” and [He has enjoined,] “Set your faces [toward Him] at every place of worship, and invoke Him, putting your exclusive faith in Him. Even as He brought you forth in the beginning, so will you return.”

(7:30) A part [of humankind] He has guided, while error is fixed upon a part, for they took devils for guardians instead of Allah, and supposed they were guided.

(7:31) O Children of Adam! Put on your adornment on every place of worship, and eat and drink, but do not waste; indeed He does not like the wasteful.

(7:32) Say, “Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah which He has brought forth for His servants, and the good things of [His] provision?” Say, “These are, on the Day of Resurrection, exclusively

for the faithful in the life of this world.” Thus do We elaborate the communications for a people who have knowledge.

(7:33) Say, “My Lord has only forbidden indecencies, the outward among them and the inward ones, and sin and undue aggression, and that you should ascribe to Allah partners for which He

has not sent down any authority, and that you should attribute to Allah what you do not know.”

(7:34) There is a [preordained] time for every nation: when their time comes, they shall not defer it by a single hour nor shall they advance it.

(7:35) O Children of Adam! If there come to you messengers from among yourselves, recounting to you My communications, then those who are Godwary and righteous will have no fear, nor will they grieve.

(7:36) But those who deny Our communications and are disdainful of them, they shall be the inmates of the Fire and they shall remain in it [forever].

Introduction

The previous section was a detailed account of the story of prostration and Adam’s garden, which is also elaborately discussed in Sūrah al-

Baqarah [2:30-39]. The same story is mentioned concisely in Sūrah Ṭā-Hā [20:115-116]. Matching these verses together, we can deduce, after some contemplation, that whereas the verses in Sūrah Ṭā-Hā are addressed to Adam specifically, the current set of verses generalize them to all his descendants, where the verses begin with: O Children of Adam. This complies with what we saw in the previous section, where the story was presented in a more general way [than in Sūrah Ṭā-Hā].

There are four verses here which begin with: O Children of Adam.

Three of them [verses 26, 27 and 31] generalize God’s initial addresses to Adam in Sūrah Ṭā-Hā. There He warns Adam against Satan’s temptations and tell him about being provided with food, drink and clothes in

the garden: We said, “O Adam! This is indeed an enemy of yours and your mate’s. So do not let him expel you from paradise, or you will be miserable. Indeed you will neither be hungry in it nor naked. Indeed you will neither be thirsty in it, nor suffer from the sun” (20:117-119). The fourth verse [7:35] generalizes a subsequent verse in Sūrah Ṭā-Hā: Then, should any guidance come to you from Me… (20:123).

Therefore, God’s initial directives to Adam [in Sūrah Ṭā-Hā] are generalized to all his descendants [here], and from them the verses conclude

a set of laws and instructions. This shows that what is legislated here in concise and general terms are universal commands that are part of all religions without any exception [because they are equally extended to all descendants of Adam]. We can also deduce that the general laws that govern the life and afterlife of any person, including the determinents of their felicity or wretchedness, stem from that initial story [of Adam]. Hence, the story of Adam [mentioned in the previous set of verses] is the root, and the laws and system [mentioned in the current set of verses] are its branches. The story of Adam is like a table of contents which presents the elaborate discussions that are to follow.

Commentary

(7:26) O Children of Adam! We have certainly sent down to you garments (libāsan) to cover your shameful parts, and adornments (rīshan).

Yet the garment of Godwariness—that is better. That is [one] of Allah’s signs, so that they may take admonition.

Libās is “something that can be worn to cover the body.” It is originally constructed as a verbal noun: labisa, yalbasu, labsan, libsan and

libāsan [where the last three terms are verbal nouns, meaning “wearing, clothing”]. Rīsh means “something that is beautiful.” It is derived from the “feathers” (rīsh) of birds in the sense that their beauty and adornment. Rīsh is also used for appliances and furniture.

Apparently what is meant by “sending down” garments and adornments is “creating” them. The same usage is seen elsewhere in the Qur’an:

and We sent down iron, in which there is great might and uses (57:25); and He has sent down for you eight mates of the cattle (39:6). This is based on the verse: There is not a thing but that its sources are with Us, and We do not send it down except in a known measure (15:21). It means that God has “sent down” garments and adornments from some hidden source that is “with Him” to the visible world. This process is called khalq (creation) [in its etymological sense, which means taqdīr (measurement)].

Garments are a product of human manufacturing and fabrication, but not their primary material such as cotton, wool and silk. We extract, spin, weave, sew and cut these things until we make garments out of them which are suitable for wearing. Hence, garments and adornments are produced by humans, yet the verse attributes them to God. This attribution is similar to the verse: butAllah has created you and whatever you make (37:96).

The existence of anything traces to God and can be attributed to Him, whether that thing occurs through human activity, or occurs through other means and instruments, including the essential properties of different species like the growing of plants from the earth, the yellow color of

gold, and the sweetness of honey. All means and instruments, including all their properties and impacts, trace back to God, Who encompasses all of their existential properties.

Meanwhile, not all events can be called “created” in the same sense. Everything goes back to God except the aspects of deficiency, evil and sin in His creation, because these things are in fact a lack of creation of good, or a violation of God’s command. Hence, they are not created [as things that are brought to existence primarily]. Rather, they are aspects of some deficiency in human deeds, whether inward or outward. We have repeatedly discussed this idea in different places in this book.1

The verse describes the purpose of garments as: to cover your shameful parts. This refers to the need which makes humans go after clothes:

to cover their body parts which would be shameful to them to reveal. As

1 See volume 3, pp. 243-244 (under verses 2:216-218), and volume 9, pp. 13ff (under verses 4:77-80) of the English translation. (Trans.)

with adornment, humans go after them to embellish themselves, which is something beyond the primary need for clothing. This verse implies God’s favor upon humans for guiding them to manufacture garments and adornments. As some exegetes have said, we can also infer from this verse that it is permissible to wear clothes for beauty.

Yet the garment of Godwariness—that is better. That is [one] of Allah’s signs, so that they may take admonition: Here the verse makes a transition from physical garments to a spiritual garment. The former cover the

body parts that would make one ashamed if they are revealed. Similarly, the latter covers inner defects that would make one ashamed if they are revealed. These defects include polytheism and all other sins. This spiritual garment is Godwariness, which is God’s advice and command to us.

The psychological pain and humiliation that one suffers due to a disclosure of any defect—whether that is physical or spiritual—is of the same nature. However, the appearance of inner defects is more intense, bitter and lasting, because then one has to face God and be accountable to Him, and because they result in a fire which will overspread the hearts

(104:7). This is why the garment of Godwariness is better than the physical garments.

… That is [one] of Allah’s signs, so that they may take admonition: This sentence complements the previous part of the verse. It means that the physical garment is a sign of God. We must reflect on the fact that we have some private parts which we should cover with clothes, because their disclosure would grieve us. Then we should infer that we also have some spiritual defects that we must cover, because their disclosure would grieve us in like manner. We will then realize that we must, a fortiori, cover these hidden defects. These defects are our moral vices and evil habits, and the garment that we need to cover them is the garment of Godwariness. This is what God has commanded us, and has explained it to us through the tongue of His prophets. This garment is necessary for us to remove our [spiritual] need.

Here is a list of how other exegetes have interpreted the garment of Godwariness:

(1) It means belief and good deeds.

(2) It means having a decent appearance as a righteous person.

(3) It means ḥayāʾ (shame, modesty).

(4) It means the garment of worship and asceticism, which is typically coarse woolen clothes.

(5) It means Islam.

(6) It means what is worn in battles.

(7) It means anything that covers the private parts.

(8) It means fear of God.

(9) It means what the Godwary will wear on the Day of Resurrection. That is better than all garments in this world.

The readers would certainly agree that none of these views is quite concordant with the context and flow of the verse.

(7:27) O Children of Adam! Do not let Satan tempt you, like he expelled your parents from paradise, stripping them of their garments to expose to them their shameful parts. Indeed he sees you—he and his hosts—whence you do not see them. We have indeed made the devils guardians of those who have no faith.

The repetition of O Children of Adam at the beginning of this verse makes it independent of the last verse, but semantically it follows the same thread—as we can see, there is again reference made to shameful parts. The meaning is: “You humans have some shameful parts that can only be covered by the garment of Godwariness, and We have dressed you in this garment by the innate makeup and creation (fiṭrah) that We have given you. So beware lest Satan deceives you and takes away this garment from you, as he took it away from your parents in the garden, in order to expose to them their shameful parts. Indeed We have made the devils guardians over those who follow them and do not believe in Our signs.”

This means that what Satan did to Adam and Eve in the garden—that is, stripping them of their garments to expose to them their shameful parts— symbolizes what he does to all humans: he strips them of their innate garment of Godwariness through temptation. Hence, all individuals are in the “garden of felicity” as long as they do not fall for this temptation. Once they fall for Satan’s deception, God expels them from that garden. … Indeed he sees you—he and his hosts—whence you do not see them…: This sentence emphasizes the previous warning. It says that Satan’s work is so subtle that one does not realize it, and so hidden that one does not sense it. One only sees oneself in the process, without realizing that there is another being or force beyond him who commands him to do evil and leads him toward wretchedness.

… We have indeed made the devils guardians of those who have no faith: This is another emphasis on the previous prohibition. The control and authority that the devils have over humans is inasmuch as tempting and deceiving them. Once one falls for their temptation and deception, they take control of the person as they wish. This is seen in God’s

addresses to Iblīs: “Entice whomever of them you can with your voice; and rally against them your cavalry and your infantry, and share with them in wealth and children, and make promises to them!” But Satan promises them nothing but delusion. “As for My servants, you shall have no authority over them.” And your Lord suffices as trustee (17:64-65); Indeed he does not have any authority over those who have faith and put their trust in their Lord

(16:99); Indeed as for My servants you do not have any authority over them, except the perverse who follow you (15:42). Matching these verses with the current verse, we can deduce that the devils have no authority over the believers, although they may sometimes be tempted by the devils. Satan has no authority over those believers who trust in God [16:99], who are described as My servants in the other verse [17:65]. This means that Satan’s authority only encompasses those who do not believe.

What is meant by “lack of faith” here is not simply atheism or polytheism [which includes passive unbelief], but it is rejecting the signs and

communications of God [actively and deliberately]. This is a more specific and restricted meaning than the general sense of unbelief. Our evidence for this specific interpretation is found in God’s addresses to humankind in this story: We said, “Get down from it, all together! Then, should any guidance come to you from Me… But those who are faithless and deny Our signs, they shall be the inmates of the Fire and they shall remain in it [forever]” (2:38-39); But those who deny Our communications and are disdainful of them, they shall be the inmates of the Fire and they shall remain

in it [forever] (7:36).

(7:28) When they commit an indecency, they say, “We found our fathers practicing it, and Allah has enjoined it upon us.” Say, “Indeed Allah does not enjoin indecencies. Do you attribute to Allah what you do not know?”

Whereas in the previous verses God addressed all children of Adam, in this verse He addresses the Prophet in particular, since He wants to then deduce certain points that specifically apply to the Prophet’s nation. We had a similar transition to this in verse 7:26, where the verse began with O Children of Adam, but ended with: That is (dhālika) [one] of Allah’s signs, so that they may take admonition (7:26). That transition served the same purpose.1

What happened in the story of Adam’s garden was that their shameful parts were disclosed, which led to their expulsion from the garden. This shows that God is not pleased with indecent acts by the people. Following the same theme, this verse talks about the polytheists committing indecencies, justifying it by the practice of their fathers, and claiming that God

has ordered them to do so. God commands His Messenger to respond to them by clarifying that He never orders indecency, and reminding them that their claim is not based on knowledge, but is a false imputation to God. The story of the garden is a proof for this.

The verse quotes two arguments from the polytheists to support and justify their practice: (1) that their fathers did the same; (2) that God has enjoined them to do so. Only the second argument is relevant to the above generalization from the story of Adam’s garden. That is why the verse only responds to that. Their first statement is also fiawed and not admitted by God, but it is not addressed here since it goes beyond the theme

of these verses. God has refuted it in many other verses in the Qur’an, such as: What, even if their fathers neither applied any reason nor were guided?! (2:170).

Several exegetes have said that this verse—When they commit an indecency… (7:28)—refers to a common custom in the pre-Islamic era among the Arabs, where they used to circumambulate the Holy House

1 The demonstrative pronoun dhālika (as used at the end of verse 7:26) is used in second person singular addresses. The author’s point is that these verses begin with general addresses to all humans, but then narrow down to make specific statements about the audience of the Qur’an at the time of revelation. (Trans.)

naked. Their reason for this was: “We do not want to circumambulate in clothes in which we have sinned, but we want to circumambulate just as our mothers gave birth to us.” It is narrated from al-Farrāʾ that they used to take some pieces of leather called ḥawf, or pieces of wool called rahṭ, and wrap it around their waist. Women used to cover their fronts with a strap or something else. Then they would chant:

Today shall appear part of it or all,

But to look at what appears is by no means halal.

This custom was common among them until the Prophet prohibited them from doing so after the conquest of Mecca, when he sent ʿAlī

to recite the opening verses of Sūrah al-Barāʾah [9:1-16] in Mecca. The Prophet—and/or some Muslims—sometimes blamed the polytheists for this practice, but they justified it by saying: We found our fathers practicing it, and Allah has enjoined it upon us. Thus God refuted their claim and

rebuked them by revealing: Indeed Allah does not enjoin indecencies. Do you attribute to Allah what you do not know?

The above interpretation of the verse is in fact quite possible, and there are some indications in the verse to support it. One indication is that their act is called al-faḥshāʾ (indecency), which means “a very abhorrent act.” Another indication is that they used to justify it by saying that

God has ordered them to do so. This means that the act must have been an indecency that was committed in the context of some worship, which matches naked circumambulation. Nevertheless, the verse uses the word al-faḥshāʾ in an unrestricted form [indicated by the article al-]. Therefore, it can have multiple instances and applications, including what they used to do, as well as other similar practices that are found among the people, especially in our time and age.

(7:29) Say, “My Lord has enjoined justice (bil-qis.),” and [He has enjoined,] “Set your faces [toward Him] at every place of worship, and invoke Him, putting your exclusive faith in Him. Even as He brought you forth in the beginning, so will you return.”

The last verse denied the claim that God has enjoined indecencies, and stated that such a claim is not rooted in anything that God has revealed. Hence it is a calumny against Him and a statement made without knowledge. This verse complements that negation by affirming what God has

in fact enjoined: Say, “My Lord has enjoined justice”…. The last verse was about faḥshāʾ (indecency), which means a severely vile act, which would necessarily be on either extremum of excess or defect. That is why this verse contrasts it by qisṭ (justice, balance). Al-Rāghib says:

Qisṭ means “a fair share,” which makes it synonymous with niṣf and niṣfah (half, equal share). God says: that He may reward those who have faith and do righteous deeds with justice (bil-qisṭ)

(10:4); Maintain the weights with justice (bil-qisṭ) (55:9). Qasṭ means usurping the fair share (qisṭ) of someone else, which is the same as jawr (oppression, injustice, wrong). Iqsāṭ means giving the fair share (qisṭ) of someone else, which is the same as inṣāf (fairness, equity). When one takes something wrongly, it is said:

qasaṭa al-rajul (he wronged); and when one observes justice, it is said: aqsaṭa (he was fair). Thus the Qur’an says: As for the unjust (al-qāsiṭūn), they will be firewood for hell (72:15); and do justice (aqsiṭū); indeed Allah loves the just (al-muqsiṭīn) (49:9).

The meaning is, “Say: My Lord has commanded that you must observe fairness, follow the middle path in all affairs, and abstain from the two extremes of excess and lack. So be just and return [to your Lord]. Establish yourselves in every place of worship of God, and call Him with a sincere religion. Do not associate anyone with Him in your worship, whether that is an idols or your fathers—through blindly following them. This is justice (qisṭ) in worship.”

… and [He has enjoined,] “Set your faces (wujūhakum, plural of wajh) [toward Him] at every place of worship…”: The conjunction “and” apparently shows that the first part of the verse implies an imperative: “Be just and set you heart…” The wajh (face) of something is the part of it that faces other things. The human face often represents the person as a whole. Setting up the “face” at every place of worship means doing justice to this act [of worship] completely, without any shortcoming. Therefore, the meaning of setting up one’s face in worship boils down to engaging in worship only and cutting oneself from every other occupation.

… Set your faces [toward Him] at every place of worship, and invoke Him, putting your exclusive faith in Him…: Based on our explanation, these two sentences together mean that one should free oneself from every occupation other than God’s service, and from any object of worship other than God. Among these “others”—from which one should sever

oneself—is worship itself. Worship is the act of paying attention [to God] not an object of attention itself. If one’s attention is directed at one’s worship, then that act is no longer “worship,” because worship means turning

one’s attention to God. Hence, when anyone worships, one must forget everything else, and must be mindful of no one but God.

Here is a list of how other exegetes have interpreted Set your faces [toward Him] at every place of worship (masjid):

(1) It means: “When you pray in any mosque, directly face the qiblah (direction of prayer).”

(2) Masjid means “time of prostration” which is the time of prayer. The meaning is: “At times of prayers face the direction that God has ordered you, which is the Kaʿbah.”

(3) “At every masjid” means that if it is the time of prayer and you are in [the vicinity of] a mosque, then pray in that mosque. Do not postpone it until you go back to your own mosque [in your neighborhood].

(4) It means: “Go to the mosque whenever there is the time to pray.” In other words, the verse commands praying in congregation.

(5) It means: “Direct your faces at God by obeying Him alone. Do not associate with Him the idols or any other partner.”

Despite their difference, none of these views is a plausible interpretation of the verse. The first three do not match the condition of Muslims in

Mecca, which is where this chapter was revealed. At the time the Kaʿbah was not the qiblah, nor did the Muslims have multiple mosques to pray in. The last view is close to our interpretation of the verse, but its problem is that it is rather an exposition of the next part of the verse about ikhlāṣ (exclusivity, sincerity, purity)—putting your exclusive faith in Him—not the part which says: Set your faces [toward Him] at every place of worship.

(7:30) A part (farīqan) [of humankind] He has guided, while error is fixed upon a part (farīqan), for they took devils for guardians instead of Allah, and supposed they were guided.

The linguistic construct of the word farīqan suggests that it functions as a ḥāl (circumstantial qualifier, participial phrase), describing the condition of the subject “you” at the end of the last verse: Even as He brought

you forth in the beginning, so will you return. In other words, the end of the last verse compares people’s end to their origin, and this verse clarifies in what sense the two stages are similar. It means: “You shall return

while you are two parties, just as you initiated while being two parties.”1 A similar analogy [between the beginning and the end] is found in the verse: Certainly you have come to Us alone, just as We created you the first time (6:94), which means: “Certainly you have come to Us alone, just as We created you the first time alone.”2 This is the clearest meaning that we can infer from the verse.

Some exegetes have claimed that farīqan cannot be a ḥāl for what is mentioned in the previous verse. Therefore, there must be another point of similarity between the two stages of their origination and end, such as being alone in both stages, issuing from dust in both stages, both stages being by God’s power, and so on. However, all these are far-fetched possibilities from the meaning of the verse. After all, why should God not

state the point of similarity, and instead mention something that is not needed, especially in a context where the intended meaning could be misunderstood? We shall explain this below, by God’s will.

What is meant by “beginning”—in Even as He brought you forth in the beginning—is only the very onset of human life in this world, not the entire span of human life in this world in contrast to their life in the hereafter. The meaning is: “He created you in this world, where He guided a

party of you, while another party were destined for deviation. Thus you shall return [while being composed of these two groups].” This is effectively the same as an interpretation offered by some exegetes: “You will

be resurrected in the same state that you died: those who died with īmān

1 Ḥāl always implies the meaning of “while.” It describes a subject who does an act while being in a certain state (ḥāl), or an object which is acted upon while it is in a certain state. (Trans.)

2 In other words, verse 6:94 clearly states how the two stages are similar: in that

you are alone and on your own. (Trans.)

(belief, faith) shall be resurrected with īmān, and those who died with kufr (disbelief, infidelity) shall be resurrected with kufr.”

When we speak of the “beginning” of something that stretches over time, what is meant is the first part of it where it starts, not all of it.1 Here,

the audience are all people. Hence, their “beginning” would be when humankind was first created and appeared. Moreover, this verse builds on the previous verses about the origination of humankind, where God says: Certainly We created you, then We formed you, then We said to the angels, “Prostrate before Adam” (7:11). Therefore, as He brought you forth in the beginning refers to how the previously mentioned creation of humankind unfolded. The idea of having two groups from the beginning was already alluded to in God’s address to Satan: Begone hence, blameful, banished! Whoever of them follows you, I will surely fill hell with you all (7:18). This verse shows a divine decree that humankind shall divide into two groups: one group are those who are guided on the straight path, and one group are those upon whom error is fixed. This is how He originated humans, and that is how they shall return.

A more explicit mention of this is found in another verse, where God says [to Satan]: This is a straight path incumbent upon Me. Indeed as for My servants you do not have any authority over them, except the perverse who follow you (15:41-42). The “straight path” mentioned here refers to a definite decree from God that people shall divide into two groups. One group are outside Satan’s authority, and those are the ones whom God guides. Another group are the perverse who follow Satan, for whom it is prescribed to deviate from the truth due to submitting to Satan and following him. The Qur’an says: About him [Satan] it has been decreed that

should anyone take him for a friend, he will lead him astray, and conduct him toward the punishment of the Blaze (22:4). This verse suggests that their misguidance is a consequence of their following the devil and taking him as a friend, not vice versa.

Another example is: Said He, “The truth is that—and I speak the truth— I will surely fill hell with you and all those who follow you” (38:84-85). Here again we see that God has decreed that humans shall divide into two groups. It is for the same reason that after the story of the fall, God says:

1 This is the second time the author is stating this point. This sensitivity and emphasis is to avoid the impression of jabr (compulsion, determinism, predestination). (Trans.)

Get down both of you from it… Then, should (fa-immā) any guidance come to you from Me, those who follow My guidance will not go astray, nor will they be miserable.But whoever disregards My remembrance, his shall be a wretched life, and on the Day of Resurrection We shall raise him blind

(20:123-124). Here, the letter fāʾ (then, so, therefore) shows that the division of humankind into two groups was a direct consequence of their

appearance on earth. It should also be noted that “blindness” here means “error” [that is, being blind of guidance].

Given the above Qur’anic evidence, we can interpret the current verses of discussion—as He brought you forth in the beginning, so will you return… (7:29-30)—as a justification for the previous commands [at the beginning of verse 7:29]. The meaning would be: “Observe justice in your actions and dedicate yourselves to God exclusively, because when God created you humankind, He decreed that you shall split into two groups: a group that is guided by Him, and a group that deviates from the path. You will return as He originated you, one group having been guided by, Him and another group being overcome by error because of accepting the authority of devils. Therefore, you should be just and sincere so that you may be among those who are guided through God’s instruction, not those who go astray through adopting the authority of devils.”

Our suggested interpretation here makes the verse comparable to the verse: Everyone has a direction to which he turns; so take the lead in the good works. Wherever you may be, Allah will bring you all together (2:148). This verse, on the one hand, states that everyone has a specific goal that they seek, until they reach its definite goal of either felicity or wretchedness. On the other hand, it orders the people to take the lead in the good

works. If the felicity or wretchedness of every person is already certain, then this order would not make sense. Therefore, what is meant is: “Every one of you should necessarily turn toward a specific direction—which will either lead you to paradise or to hell. Hence, hasten to do good deeds so that you may be among those who are directed toward felicity, not among the other group.”

We can interpret the current verses of discussion [7:29-30] in like manner: “You shall return in two groups just as God brought you into being in two groups according to His definite decree. Therefore, you must be just in your actions and sincerely dedicated to God, so that you may be among those who are guided on the return journey, not among those for whom error is established.”

Finally, it is possible to say that the last part of verse 7:29 and the entire verse 7:30—Even as He brought you forth in the beginning…—compose an independent statement that is not primarily a continuation of the first part of verse 7:29. But even in that case, this statement would still bear a subtle hint to the previous command to justice and sincerity, as it springs to mind based on the context.1

… for they took devils for guardians…: This statement explains why error was ordained and established for them: while error is fixed upon a part. It is as if the decree of being destined for error and loss is conditional on the person accepting the guardianship of Satan. This is confirmed by

1 The author has bundled the last sentence in verse 7:29—Even as He brought you forth in the beginning, so will you return—with verse 7:30 as one unit. His reason for doing so is that the sentence in verse 7:29 compares the “beginning” to the “return” without specifying in what sense they are similar, which necessitates the discussion to continue in the next verse. However, the sentence in verse 7:29 seems to have a complete meaning on its own. It is not about the how of the beginning and the return, but about their actual occurrence. An almost identical sentence is mentioned elsewhere, using the same verbs, about the creation as a whole, not the creation of humankind in particular: as We began the first creation, so We shall return it (21:104). This verse shows that the comparison between the beginning and the return is complete in itself, because it is about the very existence and creation of things, not about some aspect of their existence and creation. The following two verses also convey the same message: Say, “He will revive them who produced them the first time” (36:79); Your creation and your resurrection are not but as of a single soul (31:28). Humans have such a makeup—called the fiṭrah (primal nature, innate disposition)—that does not allow them to submit to anything other than the truth, or seek anything other than their good and happiness. The problem is in the application of this disposition. If one is supported by divine grace, they will pursue the right path, seek the actual truth, and achieve it at the end. They end up serving God alone, in which lies the eternal happiness and good life that they wish. Sometimes, however, one deviates from the straight path and chooses falsehood instead of truth, evil instead of good, and wretchedness instead of felicity. They adopt their desires as their god, serve the Devil, submit to the idols, indulge in the material adornments and glamour of this world, and take the world as their final goal [instead of a means and passage]. Nevertheless, they do so only because of supposing that this is what they should do; that this is the right way and the correct thing to do. In other words, they choose falsehood supposing that it is the truth; they do evil assuming that it is good;

and they pursue wretchedness thinking that it leads to happiness. This means that the innate human cognition [which is always oriented toward true beliefs and good deeds] is preserved without any change, but the person has mismatched it in its practical applications. God says: O you who

were given the Book! Believe in what We have sent down confirming what is with you, before We blot out the faces and turn them backwards (4:47). It is impossible that one would choose and follow falsehood, wretchedness and loss through falsehood, wretchedness and loss. The Qur’an

says: the origination of Allah according to which He originated humankind. There is no altering Allah’s creation (30:30). Any being that works in

the universe—including humankind—only inclines toward a goal or act which is in harmony with its essence and beneficial for it. If we see any counter examples for this, it is only a prima facie observation, not the fact of the matter.

The above is what we can say about these verses after a complete analysis and deep reflection: as He brought you forth in the beginning, so will you return. A part [of humankind] He has guided, while error is fixed upon a part… (7:29-30). Our interpretation is based on the word farīqan [in verse 7:30] functioning as a ḥāl (circumstantial qualifier, participial phrase) for the verb so will you return. That is, the beginning and the return are compared with one another in the sense that in both cases the people will be classified into two groups. This meaning is applicable whether the last part of verse 7:29 [as He brought you forth…] is connected to the previous part of the verse—as a justification for it—or not.

However, most exegetes have agreed that the two parties mentioned in verse 7:30 only describe the state of return of the people, not their state of beginning. They have assumed there to be another basis for comparing the beginning with the return [in verse 7:29]—which is not mentioned here [in verse 7:30]. One exegete has interpreted “beginning” as “the entire round of worldly life.” As we said above, this cannot be true, and we shall discuss it further below. Since these verses are surrounded by commands and prohibitions, they imply the free will of humankind. That is why the exegetes have opted for the above interpretations—because they did not want to fall for jabr (compulsion, determinism, predestination). However, our readers would concur that our interpretation does not necessitate jabr given our thorough analysis.

W hat these narrations and verses mean is not to assert that felicity and wretchedness are among the essential properties of people—in the sense that evenness is an essential property of number four. This possibility is totally out of the question. Such essential property can be interpreted in two ways, both of which are problematic. (1) Felicity or wretchedness is a necessary concomitant of one’s essence at the level of mental image. W hat is meant here is that the mind derives the concepts of felicity and wretchedness from what happens in the external world, and applies them to its

Such essential property is devoid of any real impact or practical significance. (2) Felicity or wretchedness is a necessary, inseparable and independent requirement of one’s substance. This means that God’s job is only to bring out what is hidden in the person’s essence, which entails a limitation on God’s absolute dominion and a restriction of His authority. That would be contrary to the Qur’an, the sunnah, and reason.

This idea contradicts reason because rational people conduct their affairs based on the assumption that education and training have an impact on the souls. They are unanimous about this principle, and agree on classifying actions as good or evil, and assigning praise and blame to them.

It is also against the idea that God has completed His argument against the people through sending religions, scriptures and messengers.1 If one’s actions and destiny are already embedded in one’s substance as essential properties—meaning properties that are impossible to be separated from the person—then it does not make sense to offer any proof, argument or guidance to the person. There is no consistent way of conceiving this. The picture the Holy Qur’an draws for us also confirms a rational system of human life based on the free will of the people. The Qur’an says

that God created humans from dust, then He made their progeny from an extract of a base fluid (32:8). He makes them grow in a splendid fashion, until He blesses them with maturity and reason, whereby they act voluntarily and can distinguish between good and bad, virtue and vice, benefit

and loss, obedience and disobedience, reward and punishment. He then

blesses them by directing His religious obligations to them. Those who follow their reason and obey their Lord with respect to His commands and prohibitions will be happy and rewarded with the best of rewards. Those who oppose their reason, follow their desires, and disobey their Lord will be wretched and will taste the consequence of their deeds. This life is an abode of test and trial: today is the time for action, and tomorrow is the time for retribution.

As one can see, this Qur’anic picture is based on two principles: (1) There is a difference between voluntary and involuntary acts. This is a rational, necessary statement. (2) Voluntary acts can be described as good or evil, and can win either praise and reward, or blame and punishment. This is also a rule of reason and a governing principle which gives order to human societies. Hence no rational person can deny it.

These are two indubitable and unquestionable premises which prove that felicity and wretchedness are connected to the voluntary acts of the people. Hence, there is no place whatsoever to hold that felicity and wretchedness are essential properties—in the sense that we discussed above. The Qur’anic verses and narrations in this regard do not tie people’s ends to their essences per se, but they tie people’s ends to God’s creation and existentiation.1 Nevertheless, we need to explore the meaning of these verses and narrations further.

Narrations which match the return to the beginning are abundant in number, and vary from one another in terms of their text and context, much like the verses in this regard. We can classify these narrations under five categories:

The last narration provides some explanation for the one before it, because it implies that there is some relationship between the qualities and conditions of people—in terms of being righteous or unrighteous—and the earthly matter from which they are created. This complies with our first-hand experience: different matters are inevitably different in terms of what form they can adopt1 and what effects they can cause—although this difference is at the level of preponderance (iqtiḍāʾ), not complete causation (ʿilliyyat tāmmah).

Therefore, if we put together what is said in these narrations—that we are made of some clay from the earth, and that our origin is either paradise or hell—we can deduce that parts of earth belong to paradise and parts of it belong to hell. Each part will certainly end up where it belongs, but the process of each part reaching where it belongs is through our doing. The earth first becomes a human, and then we either purify ourselves and thus enter paradise; or we plunge into darkness, whereby we enter hell and become fuel for the fire. This is what determines if one’s original earthen substance is congruent with heaven or hell.

The following verse bears some allusion to this idea, where the inhabitants of paradise will say [after they enter paradise on the Day of Resurrection]: All praise belongs to Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us and made us heirs to the earth, that we may settle in paradise wherever we may wish (39:74). Apparently what is meant by “earth” here is the very earth where humans live, where they die, and whence they are raised. This “earth” is used interchangeably with “paradise” in this verse. Another verse that refers to the same point is: The day the earth is transformed into another earth and the heavens [as well] (14:48). In short, apparently what is meant by “the clay of paradise” and “the clay of hell” in the narrations is “the clay which will become part of paradise or hell in future.” This interpretation is especially strengthened by certain expressions such as “the clay of ʿIlliyyūn” and “the clay of Sijjīn” [in the first narration], as well

The same can be said about wretchedness, where wretchedness in knowledge means abandoning one’s reason, and relying on illusions and superstitions which embellish the forces of appetite and anger to the person. Likewise, wretchedness in practice means indulging in material pleasures, yielding to carnal desires, and defiantly rejecting any truth that does not match one’s interests. There is yet another possible explanation for these narrations, which is more advanced, requires a high level of intellectual precision, and is based on a profound understanding of metaphysical principles. The integral element in one’s felicity or wretchedness is one’s degree of consciousness, which is one’s intellectual realization. This is something immaterial and unbound by the laws and restrictions of material phenomena, including time. Time is a measure of change, and as such it is an exclusive aspect of material events.1 We see a material substance transforming from potentiality to actualization, and thus conclude that “felicity occurs after one’s

actions.” However, this is only when we look at it from the perspective of the material substance. Otherwise, felicity in itself is not temporal. It is not something that exists in one time or another because it is not a material reality. Therefore, “prior felicity” and “future felicity” are identical; the distinction comes in only when we map out the movement of a

time-bound entity.

This is exactly what happens when we talk about the acts of God occurring “in time.” For instance we say, “God created Zayd on such a day”; “That is when God drowned Noah’s tribe”; “He rescued Jonah’s people in the xth century”; or “He appointed Muḥammad as prophet in year y.” In these examples, God’s action is temporal because we are not looking at it in its entirety. What happens in time is only one aspect of God’s doing, divested of the other aspects. Otherwise, in the broad scheme of things, God is the creator of an event with all its features, including its time and the preparatory changes which give rise to it. This means that God’s act is (sabab, ʿillah) is only seemingly and apparently so, but not in reality. All forces

and factors in creation are like sleeves which cover the hand which extends through them and effects changes. They are all expressions, extensions and reflections of the only real cause. There is no contradiction, nor any real duality, in the working of different members of the same body. It is a single subject which employs different organs to what he wills, according to their capacity and based on his wisdom. This is called “vertical agency” (fāʿiliyyah ṭūliyyah). (Trans.)

We qualify God’s acts by time because it is in a sense united with a temporal incident that we observe from our perspective in the temporal world. Another example is when we talk about our comprehension as a temporal event, like when we say, “Today I learnt this and that” or “Now I see.”

Knowledge qua knowledge is not temporal. Given the most apparent meaning of Qur’an and hadith, there is a physical paradise and a physical hell in the hereafter. The Imam added at the end: “That is why a believer is born to a disbeliever, and a disbeliever is born to a believer.”2 (3) Imam al-Ṣādiq said: God ordered some water: “Be sweet and agreeable so that I may create from you My paradise and the people of My obedience.” He ordered some other water: “Be salty and bitter so that I may create from you My fire and the people of My disobedience.” Then He applied the two waters on clay.3 There are numerous other narrations—from Imams ʿAlī, al-Bāqir, al-Ṣādiq and others—which convey the same idea as each of the above. We quoted these three as a sample. These narrations can be matched with

No female conceives or delivers except with His knowledge, and no elderly person advances in years, nor is anything diminished of his life, but it is [recorded] in a Book. The first verse [35:11] is about how individuals differ from one another despite being of the same species and having common enjoyments and benefits. Then the second verse [35:12] provides an example to clarify and illustrate this.

Elsewhere God says: and We made every living thing out of water

(21:30). Another verse in this regard is: It is He who created the human being from water, then invested him with ties of blood and marriage, and your Lord is all-Powerful (25:54). We shall discuss these verses in their own place.

This set of narrations can be classified into two categories:

(1) Some of them say that the two types of water—one being sweet and agreeable, and one being salty and bitter—were applied to the clay which was the substance of humankind’s creation. That is the source of difference in the substance of people. This boils down to the previous set of narrations about the differences of people being traceable to to their clay. Hence, the same explanations that we provided there would be applicable to these narrations.

(2) Some of them say that creation as a whole—including the creation of humankind and other things, even paradise and hell—is from

water, and the felicity and wretchedness of the people is because they are made of different waters. In other words, the differences in creation are rooted in being created of either potable or briny water. This again boils down to the previous set of narrations about ṭīnah (clay, substance), and the same discussion would apply here. Hence, the first category serves to interpret the second, and all of them serve to interpret the previous set of narrations about ṭīnah.

There is also the idea that at the end, the creation will return to its origin, which was water. This is another topic which we shall discuss later in its appropriate place, by God’s will.

IV. Narrations about Creation from Light and Darkness Some narrations state that the difference of people is because they were created from either light or darkness. One example is:

Imam al-Ṣādiq said, “Indeed God created us [Ahl al-Bayt] from a light that was drawn from another light that is ingrained in the ṭīnah (clay, substance) from the top of ʿIlliyyūn (the Highest Heaven, the Elevated Record). He created the hearts of our followers (lit. shīʿah) from what He created our bodies from, and created their bodies from a lower substance. So their hearts incline

toward us because they are created from what we are created from.” The Imam then recited: No indeed! The record of the pious is indeed in ʿIlliyyūn. And what will show you what is ʿIlliyyūn?

It is a written record, witnessed by those brought near [to Allah]

(83:18-21).

He continued: “Indeed God created the heart of our enemies from a ṭīnah from Sijjīn (the Lowest Hell, the Infernal Record), and created their bodies from a lower substance. He created the hearts of their followers from what He created their bodies from;

that is why their hearts incline toward them.” Then He recited: No indeed! The record of the vicious is indeed in Sijjīn. And what will show you what is Sijjīn? It is a written record.Woe to the deniers on that day (83:7-10).1

This, and other similar narrations, reduce to the second set of narrations that we discussed above, concerning the origin of creation tracing

to either the clay of ʿIlliyyūn or the clay of Sijjīn. However, they specify that after the stage of clay, the substance of people becomes either light or darkness. Apparently light and darkness here symbolize knowledge and ignorance, respectively. A felicitous substance reflects the truths and leads to knowledge, while a wretched substance is intertwined with ignorance and blindness. This means that the ṭīnah of felicity is light. This language has its roots in the Qur’an, which frequently refers to knowledge and guidance as light, just as it refers to īmān (belief, faith) as life. God says: Is he

who was lifeless, then We gave him life and provided him with a light by which he walks among the people, like one who dwells in a manifold darkness which he cannot leave? (6:122); Allah is the Guardian of the faithful:

There are abundant other narrations which say that light was the original substance for the creation of a set of beings such as the prophets, the angels, the Tablet, the Pen, the Throne, the Pedestal, and paradise. We shall present some of these under other relevant verses, if God wills.

V. Narrations about Merging the Deeds of Good-doers and Evil-doers

Some narrations talk about the good deeds of the wretched being added to [the record] of the felicitous, and the evil deeds of the felicitous being added to the record of the wretched. One example for this is

found in part of a long narration from Imam al-Bāqir, on the authority of Ibrāhīm al-Laythī:

… Then the Imam asked me: “Tell me, Ibrāhīm, when the sun rises and shines its rays on different lands, do the ray separate from the disk?”

I said, “W hen it rises, the rays are separate [from the disk].”

“Isn’t it true,” the Imam ask, “that when it sets, the rays return and connect back to the disk?”

“Yes,” I confirmed.

He explained, “In the same way everything will return to its original substance and root. On the Day of Resurrection, God will remove anything that is congruous with our enemies (sing.

nāṣīb)—including their [dark] substance and it resulting sins and burdens—from the believers, and will add them all to our enemies [because of their essential congruence]. He will also remove anything that is congruous with the believers—including their substance and their various good deeds and efforts—from our enemies, and will add them all to the believers. Now, do you think there is any injustice and aggression in this?”

“No, O son of God’s Messenger.”

He said, “By God this is a decisive decree, a definitive rule, and clear justice. He is not questioned concerning what He does, but they are questioned (21:23). This, O Ibrāhīm,is the truth from your Lord; so do not be among the skeptics (3:60). This is a law of malakūt (God’s kingdom, angelic world).”

“O son of God’s Messenger,” I asked, “what is the law of malakūt?”

“That is the law of God, the law of His prophets, and the story of al-Khiḍr and Moses—when Moses accompanied al-Khiḍr, but al-Khiḍr told him: Indeed you cannot have patience with me! And how can you have patience about something you are not in the know of? (18:67-68). Contemplate this, Ibrāhīm, and fathom it. Moses criticized al-Khiḍr and condemned his acts, until al-Khiḍr told him, ‘Moses, I did not do that out of my own accord (18:82), but I only did that based on God’s command.’…”1 This narration corresponds to the verse: so that Allah may separate the bad ones from the good, and place the bad on one another, and pile them up together, and cast them into hell (8:37) and other verses which are mentioned in the above hadith. As one can see, this verse says that God will

separate good from evil on the Day of Resurrection and will completely distinguish between them, such that there remains good without any mix of evil, and evil without any mix of good. Then He will pile up all evil together, meaning that He gathers everything of evil nature: He will join people’s actions and results with the subjects who have done them; He will connect the branches back to their roots. The implication of this is that all virtues will be gathered at one end and connected back to pure felicity of essence, which is completely free from any tinge of wretchedness.

Likewise, all vices will be gathered at another end and connected back to their unmixed source of origination. This is what the above narration tries to explain.

When the Imam asks Ibrāhīm about the sun and its rays, he is providing a physical image for the idea that every effect is a reflection of its

cause, is of the same nature, depends on it, and is inseparable from it. The statement that “By God this is a decisive decree…” is based on the necessary congruence that exists between a subject and his actions, or between a cause and its effect. This entails that the real owner of every act is a subject whose essence is congruous with that act, not one who has no connection with the act [at the level of one’s essence]. This is despite our prima facie impression that such a judgment is unfair, because that impression is only at the surface level, based on outward senses [not based on one’s essential realization and substantial tendency].

Every act has two aspects: (1) It is a set of certain movements which

1 ʿIlal al-sharāʾiʿ.

is attributable to the subject who makes those movements. This aspect of the act belongs to the apparent actor. (2) It is described as either good or evil, either felicitous or wretched. This aspect of the act belongs to the essence which has the same moral value and quality. At this level, suppose there are two different causes, each having its distinct effect. Then suppose we find the effect of one manifesting from the other. This is impossible unless there is some mix between the two causes, where the real cause of the observed effect stands behind the apparent cause that is thought to be the source of the event. For instance, we may observe heat in water, but that is only because the water is heated by fire or sun [as the real source of heat]. The heat appears in water, but in reality it is a property of fire. One who investigates the truth would never fail to attribute an effect to its real source, as opposed to where it apparently manifests.

Based on the above clarification, we can say that good deeds belong to those who are good-doers by virtue of their essence, and have a felicitous substance. Similarly, evil deeds belong to those who are evil-doers

by virtue of their essence, and have a wretched root and substance. This is genuine justice, which shall appear in the realm of truth [that is, the hereafter] based on the reality of everything.

What is said here does not contradict verses which say: So whoever does an atom’s weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom’s weight of evil will see it (99:7-8); that no bearer shall bear another’s burden (53:38); Whatever [good] it earns is to its benefit, and whatever [evil] it incurs is to its harm (2:286). These verses assert that the consequence of every act should accrue to its doer: if the act is good, then they will be rewarded good, and if the act is evil, then they will receive evil. W hat is mentioned in these verses is correct in its own place. From a worldly point of view and conventionally speaking, “action” refers to a set of physical movements. Given this notion of action, the “actor” would obviously be the

person who makes those movements. So worldly reward and praise, or punishment and blame, would accrue to the person who does the act in this sense. This is where the above verses are applicable. However, from the point of view of reality, the true actor of an act is one whose essence is in line and harmony with the act, which is not necessarily the person who makes the outward movements called “action.” Therefore, saying that the act and its good or evil consequences belong to the essence from which it originated is not a violation of these verses, because we are not ascribing the act to a source where it does not belong. In other words, we have two laws at two levels, with a vertical relationship1 between them: (1) an apparent law which governs our social interactions in this world; and (2) a hidden law which the Imam referred to as “the law of malakūt.” As we have repeatedly said, the Day of Resurrection is a day when the secrets are examined [86:9], when the truth manifests and nothing conceals it anymore. That realm is where the law of malakūt comes into play and connects every event to its real subject. That is when everything returns to its origin. God says: and there will appear to them from Allah what they had never reckoned (39:47); You were certainly oblivious of this. We have removed your veil from you, and so your sight is acute today (50:22); We will make their descendants join them, and We will not stint anything from [the reward of] their deeds (52:21); But surely they will carry their own burdens and other burdens along with their own burdens (29:13).

Here we can see why the law of malakūt is specifically designated to the Day of Resurrection, and not to the barzakh (the intermediate realm between this life and the Resurrection). The barzakh—which lies between one’s death and the Resurrection—is also a time of retribution and among “the days of God” [14:5]. However, the Qur’an counts it as an extension of people’s stay on the earth and this world, as one can infer from these verses: He will say, “How many years did you remain on earth?” They will say, “We remained for a day, or part of a day; yet ask those who keep the count.” He will say, “You only remained a little; if only you had known”

(23:112-114); And on the day when the Hour sets in the guilty will swear that they had remained only for an hour. That is how they were used to lying [in the world]. But those who were given knowledge and faith will say, “Certainly you remained in Allah’s Book until the Day of Resurrection. This is the Day of Resurrection, but you did not know” (30:55-56). Our life in the barzakh is like a remainder of our worldly life, and thus it is subject to some of the same laws. In the barzakh people are still in the process of being filtered and purified, in their way to their ultimate felicity or wretchedness. The decisive decree [of attaching actions to their real actors] requires total congruence and a pure essence, which is realized only after the barzakh.

Given the above explanations, we can now understand another important idea which is mentioned in the Qur’an and hadith: that God rewards the good deeds of disbelievers in this world, but in the hereafter their actions will be void, no scale will be set up for them on the Day of Resurrection [18:105], and they shall have nothing but fire at that point. The reader should reflect on this.

God’s Actions are not Open to Question

In the above narration, the Imam quoted the verse, He is not questioned concerning what He does, but they are questioned (21:23) as a justification for what he said about the law of malakūt (God’s kingdom, angelic world). When someone does an act, makes a judgment, or utters a speech, we may ask the person to justify it for us by explaining the correspondence between the reality and his action or speech. Such questions are applicable when we are dealing with two things that are distinct and separable from one another: an action or speech on the one hand, and the truth on the other hand. There is room for question in such cases until it is clarified that what the person did or said matches reality. However, if the person’s action, judgment or statement is the reality itself, then there is no room for question, because there is no intermediating link to connect the person’s action or speech with the fact of the matter.

When you are questioned about something that you have done, judged, or said, then you are bound to that question unless you clarify the truth behind your action, judgment, or statement. For instance, if one inquires, “Why did you hit the orphan?” or “Why did you judge that this property belongs to Zayd?” or “Why did you say that Zayd is standing?” then you are bound to that question unless you provide an explanation like “I hit the orphan to discipline him”; “Zayd inherits this property from his father”; or “I saw with my own eyes that Zayd was standing.” Meanwhile, there are other statements that are not open to question, such as: “Four is even”; “Ten is greater than five”; “One ceases to be alive if his head is chopped off.” The reason is that these statements are the very reality of the matter, not something to be matched and verified with the truth. Hence, it does not make sense to ask, “Why is four even?” or “What makes ten greater than five?” W hen the complete cause of an event is realized, then the event will inevitably occur. In such cases, it is vain to ask “Why did this effect come to be?” because its efficient cause and final cause are there.1 In the case of God, His actions are the very realm of existence, and His speech is the very external reality. There is no other reality to corroborate His acts and speech. That is why there is no place for asking “why” and “how” with respect to Him. God’s act is the reality with which we assess the truth of all our beliefs and actions. We infer truths from the external world, which is the making of God. Hence, our inferences about the truth have no rule over His acts, but are rather deduced from His acts. The two are concomitant in the sense that our sense of truth [in beliefs] and right [in actions] follows His act [of creation]. The reader should reflect on this. We can explain this in a different way: God always acts through the intermediation of causes which govern the world. These causes are the means and instruments which manifest God’s acts.2 When one asks about God’s act, the person is really asking about the means through which God has acted. It reveals the person’s ignorance about the causes at work. For example, suppose Zayd dies because of a wall collapsing on him unexpectedly. Then one would ask, “Why did God kill Zayd? Why didn’t He

have mercy on his young age and his poor parents?” So they explain to him that Zayd died because the wall collapsed on him. Then he would ask, “Why did the wall collapse on him?” They tell him that the wall’s foundation had become weak and unsupportive due to rain; that is why it could not carry the weight of the wall anymore, and it so happened

In the above narration, the Imam mentioned “the law of God and the law of His prophets…” This refers to God’s judgment and decree, and the judgment of His prophets with His permission. God’s decree and judgment is based on the truth and the fact of the matter in the real world,

The above should clarify how good deeds and their consequences are added to good essences which have a substance of light, and how evil deeds and their consequences belong to evil essences which have a substance of darkness. Also, our explanation about the verse, He is not questioned concerning what He does, but they are questioned (21:23) should clarify another series of questions that may potentially arise here. One may ask: “Why is it that good essences which have a substance of light are tied to good deeds and good consequences? Why is it that evil essences which have a substance of darkness are tied to sins and evil consequences? Why do good deeds result in eternal bliss and everlasting paradise? Why do evil deeds result in God’s punishment and hell?”2 The answer is: There is a necessary existential connection between these essences and what issues from them in the real world. It is not an arbitrary assignment based on a social contract, even though in religious language it is sometimes expressed in a way that is similar to our

It is an essential property of a good or evil source to have a consequence which is congruent with it, and essential properties are not open

to question.2 However, the idea that the essential property of a being is inseparable from it does not mean that the being is an independent cause of that effect. It does not mean that the beings can necessitate their essential consequences and bind them to themselves independently of God. The Qur’an rejects this notion. Rather, what necessitates these consequences is that they are part of God’s doing, and His acts are not open

God refers to this necessary consequence using an example in the verse: The good land—its vegetation comes out by the permission of its Lord, and as for that which is bad, it does not come out except sparsely (7:58). The verse adds by the permission of its Lord as a qualification to clarify that no being is independent of God in effecting its essential properties.
